# Excessive Leaking from Injectors on a Slipped Timing Chain

When a timing chain slips five notches on a Peugeot or CitroÃ«n 1.6 HDi, the immediate concern is often whether the engine will start. In your specific case, the engine cranks and runs, but the symptomsâthick white smoke everywhere, two litres of diesel in the oil after only two minutes of operation, and severe injector drippingâare telling a different story. The chain slip itself did not break; it simply lost synchronization, allowing the camshafts to rotate relative to the crankshaft beyond their designed limits. This mechanical shift is the root cause of the catastrophic fuel dilution you are witnessing.

The primary failure mode here is almost certainly bent push rods or damaged rocker arms. In a dual-overhead-cam (DOHC) setup like the 1.6 HDi, if the chain slips significantly on one side but not the other, or if the tensioner fails to maintain proper preload during the slip event, the valve timing shifts. However, because the cam lobes are still physically pressing down on the followers, the geometry changes drastically. If the push rods are bent or the rocker arms are cracked due to the altered leverage angles, they may fail to fully lift the intake valves.

This leads directly to the "injectors pouring diesel" observation. Diesel injection systems rely on precise timing and pressure. When an intake valve does not close completely or opens at the wrong time due to mechanical interference from a bent push rod, high-pressure fuel can be forced past the seat during the compression stroke. The injectors themselves are likely functioning correctly in terms of nozzle operation; they are delivering the commanded volume of fuel. However, because the combustion chamber is compromised by open intake valves or damaged seals, the pressure dynamics change. Instead of combusting, the fuel washes over the cylinder walls and leaks past piston rings into the crankcase. This explains why you found two litres of diesel in the oil after such a short run time. The engine is effectively pumping fuel directly into the sump because the sealing integrity of the combustion chamber has been breached by the mechanical event.

Regarding your hypothesis about injector seals or cutting the seats: do not attempt to fix this by resealing the injectors. If the intake valves are bent or the push rods are distorted, tightening the injector bolts or replacing the O-rings will not stop the fuel from being pushed out of the combustion chamber into the oil gallery. The leak path is not in the injector nozzle; it is through the cylinder head gasket area or via the valve train leakage paths.

You also mentioned blow-by and spluttering noises upon shutdown. This is consistent with low compression caused by bent valves. When you turn off the engine, the high pressure built up from the fuel injection events forces combustion gases out of the cylinders through the intake or exhaust ports (blow-by), creating the coughing sounds. The "runaway" sensation occurs because the ECU detects a lack of load or strange resistance and may adjust the fuel map, but with bent valves preventing proper scavenging, the engine struggles to stabilize.

The air leak theory regarding inlet manifold seals is unlikely to be the primary culprit given the volume of fluid involved. While a vacuum leak would cause rough idling, it would not result in massive fuel dilution or white smoke unless accompanied by valve timing issues. The camshaft sensor reading will likely be erratic due to the physical displacement of the camshafts relative to their sensors, but this is a symptom, not the source of the mechanical failure.

The repair path forward requires disassembly of the cylinder head. You must inspect the push rods and rocker arms for bending or cracking. If any component in the valve train is deformed from the chain slip event, the engine will continue to consume fuel and dilute oil until replaced. Attempting to run the engine further risks welding the valves into the guides due to the extreme heat generated by unburnt fuel injection.
